newsitem.title: KENYA: Rwanda's ousted Hutu army commanders flee in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda's ousted Hutu army commanders flee in Zaire.

text.p: The top two commanders of Rwanda's former Hutu army have fled the eastern Zairean town of Kisangani, leaving behind their demoralised troops as rebels close in on the city, a Rwandan Hutu source said on Friday.

The source told Reuters Major-General Augustine Bizimungu, commander of Rwanda's ousted 40,000-strong army, and his deputy and director of combat operations, Brigadier-General Gratien Kabiligi, left Kisangani for the capital Kinshasa five days ago.
They left ostensibly to restock on supplies for their troops who with exiled Rwandan Hutu Interahamwe militiamen have fought alongside the Zairean army against advancing Zairean rebels.

But the source said it now appeared clear the two men had abandoned their demoralised troops to fight rebels of Laurent Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire for the city, the main army base in the northeast.
Kisangani was the nerve centre of a failed government counter-offensive against the rebels. It is also Zaire's third largest city, a diamond and gold centre and a key port on river Zaire.

"It is pure fact that Bizimungu and Kabiligi have abandoned their troops. They are now in Kinshasa where they arrived five days ago," said the source, an influential member of the exiled Hutu community.
"When they left, they told their troops they were going to Kinshasa to fetch more weapons and ammunition. But it was a lie."
"It is clear that they (two generals) had clear information about advancing rebels and they decided to run like they have always done in the past four months," the source added.
He was referring to Bizimungu and Kabiligi's flight from the eastern Zairean towns of Goma and Bukavu bordering on Rwanda a week before Kabila's rebels swept in early in October last year.
Rebel chief of foreign affairs Bizima Karaha said on Thursday the rebels were 10 km (six miles) from Kisangani.

A regional military source said the rebels were virtually besieging Kisangani and would take it once their forces were consolidated around the city -- the last major stand in the northeast for Zaire's ragged army, Hutu allies and mercenaries.
A Reuters correspondent who visited the eastern Zairean jungle outpost of Punia this week found that the town's 40 or so gendarmes and local officials stationed there had long left.
The town was under the armed occupation of Hutu soldiers of the former Rwandan army, which played a leading role in the genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tusis and Hutu moderates in 1994.
Half the estimated 100,000 civilian population of the Punia and its surroundings had fled harassment by the Hutu troops.
More than half a million Hutu refugees used by the former Rwandan troops as human shields streamed back to Rwanda late last year as rebels, spearheaded by Zairean Tutsis, seized their camps.

Bizimungu and Kabiligi are widely believed to have directed the exodus of Hutus from Rwanda in 1994 as Tutsi-dominated rebels now in power advanced on the Rwandan capital to force a stop to the genocide.
The rebels have pushed towards Kisangani on three fronts from the towns of Bafwasende and Lubutu, which they captured last week, sending tens of thousands of bedraggled Hutu refugees fleeing.
They have seized a stretch of the east 1,000 km (600 miles) long since October. Zaire has repeatedly accused Burundi, Rwanda and Uganda of directly supporting the rebels. All three deny the charges.
